abstract: Adverse maternal conditions during pregnancy result in an increased risk for neuropsychiatric disorders in the offspring, although the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. We have recently shown that two distinct insults, prenatal stress (PNS) or maternal high-fat diet (mHFD), increase inflammation and oxidative stress in the brain of adolescent female mice. Here, we sought to investigate the early mechanisms underlying such effects, focusing on the placenta and fetal brain, as well as the protective effects of the antioxidant N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), in C57Bl6/N mice. We used a multi-disciplinary approach combining proteomic, metabolomic, lipidomic and histological analysis to characterize the structural and functional changes of the placenta; moreover, a targeted gene expression analysis was carried out in the brains of male and female fetuses to evaluate oxidative stress and inflammatory-related changes. Our data highlight comparable, but sex-specific, responses to the two maternal stressors, which target placenta and fetal brain, and are buffered by NAC administration. Placental function was specifically disrupted in males, with signaling pathways of cardio-metabolic risk emerging in this sex. By contrast, fetal brain was affected in females, with an increased expression of genes related to inflammation and oxidative stress. In conclusion, we provide evidence for an early origin of sex-dependent embedding of prenatal adverse experiences in different organs which might explain differential susceptibility to later disease trajectories.

Materials and methods
Ethics approval
This study was reported in conformity with ARRIVE guidelines [
17
].
All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Survey Board on behalf of the Italian Ministry of Health (license n° 893/2020-PR) and performed following the European Directive 2010/63/EU (D.Lgs. 26/2014).
Animal housing
Two-month-old C57BL/6N mice, 140 females and 70 males, were purchased from Charles River (Italy) and housed two/cage in transparent plexiglass cages (Tecniplast), in an air-conditioned room (temperature 21 ± 1 °C, relative humidity 60 ± 10%), under a reversed 12/12 h light/dark cycle with lights off from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Fresh tap-water and standard chow (energy 3.3 kcal/g, fat 17%, carbohydrate 60% and protein 23% provided by Mucedola, Italy) were continuously available.
Prenatal stressors
After three weeks of habituation, female breeders were allocated into two models of maternal stress based on a minimization approach avoiding body weight bias [
18
], as described below (Fig.
S1
).
Prenatal stress (PNS)
As expected, 50% of reproductive success led to 32 out of 70 pregnant females that were allocated into PNS or control (CTRL) groups. Females of the PNS group (
n
= 16) were individually restrained in a transparent cylinder (11.5 × 3 cm), during the dark phase, and contextually exposed to bright light as an additional stressor (6.500 lux) for 30 min, at three random times daily, from gestational day (G) 12.5 until G17.5 [
19
]. The CTRL group (
n
= 16) was left undisturbed during the entire pregnancy period, except for regular husbandry and health-tracking procedures.
Maternal HFD (mHFD)
Female breeders were fed the control diet (CD,
n
= 35) or the HFD (
n
= 35)
ad libitum
for 10 weeks before mating and throughout gestation (for a total of 13 weeks), until G17.5. The final number of pregnant dams was CD = 21 and HFD = 14. HFD (
D12331
, energy 5.56 kcal/g, fat 58%, carbohydrate 25.5% and protein 16.4%) and CD (
D12328
, energy 4.07 kcal/g, fat 10.5%, carbohydrate 73.1% and protein 16.4%) were provided by Research Diets Inc. (New Brunswick, NJ, USA).
N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC) treatment
Five weeks before mating, female breeders received either the antioxidant NAC treatment (
n
= 35 for the PNS model and
n
= 35 for the mHFD model) or tap water as vehicle (
n
= 35 for the PNS model and
n
= 35 for the mHFD model), until G17.5, for a total of 8 weeks. NAC (Sigma Aldrich, A7250) was daily administered in drinking water to yield an average dose of 1 g/kg body weight [
8
,
20
].
The final number of dams was as follows: CTRL-Vehicle
n
= 9, CTRL-NAC
n
= 7, PNS-Vehicle
n
= 9, PNS-NAC
n
= 7, CD-Vehicle
n
= 9, CD-NAC
n
= 12, HFD-Vehicle
n
= 6, HFD-NAC
n
= 8.
Mating, pregnancy and tissue collection
After 5 weeks of NAC administration (and 10 weeks on diets for the mHFD model), females were bred as previously described [
8
]. A handful of dirty sawdust (urine) from a male’s cage was added to a female’s cage every morning for 3 days so that pheromones might induce the estrus cycle. On the third day, one male was introduced into each female’s cage for 48 h. Thereafter, the weight gain of females was monitored at G7, G14 and G17.5 allowing to determine the length of gestation with a precision of ± 0.5 day. A weight gain of at least 3 g on G7 usually indicates that conception has occurred [
8
].
At G17.5, dams were sacrificed by cervical dislocation and trunk blood was collected into heparinized tubes to obtain plasma for measuring NAC levels and markers of oxidative stress. Immediately, a caesarean (c)-section was performed opening the uterine horns, the amniotic sac of each fetus was exposed and amniotic fluid carefully collected with a syringe and pooled. Fetal brains were dissected out and stored at −80 °C for gene expression analysis; fetal tails were used for sex determination. Placentas were fixed for histomorphometrical evaluations or dissected out and stored at −80 °C for proteomic, metabolomic and lipidomic analysis. Tissues were coded and analyzed in a blinded manner.
Peripheral circulating levels of NAC and markers of oxidative stress in pregnant dams
In order to assess oxidative stress in maternal plasma, we evaluated the following markers: malondialdehyde, protein carbonyls and 3-nitrotyrosin levels. NAC measurements were performed after, as previously described [
21
] with modifications. Briefly 10 µL murine plasma were spiked with 40 µL internal standard (d3-NAC, 300 nM in 90% acetonitrile) and vortexed for 30 s. To support protein precipitation, samples were stored at −20 °C for 10 min in a precooled rack and then centrifuged at 30.000 × g and 4 °C for 10 min. Next, 40 µL of supernatant were transferred into a vial with a 100 µL glass insert and 5 µL were injected into the LC system. Chromatography was performed using an ACQUITY UPLC BEH Amide column (2.1 mm × 100 mm, 1.7 µm) equipped with a VanGuard BEH Amid pre-column (2.1 mm × 5 mm, 1.7 µm). Mobile phase A consisted of acetonitrile/MilliQ water (9:1, v/v) containing 5 mM and 0.3% formic acid (v/v). Mobile phase B consisted of MilliQ water containing 25 mM ammonium formate (pH 6). Gradient elution started at 100% A and was held for 2 min. Thereafter, the proportion of solvent B was increased to 40% within 0.1 min. 40% were kept constant for 2 min until column was re-equilibrated with initial conditions until minute 6. The flow rate was constantly set at 0.25 mL/min. Samples were kept in the autosampler at 6 °C and column temperature was set at 35 °C. For detection a Waters Xevo TQ-XS was used in ESI+ mode. Monitored mass transitions were 164.1 > 122.0 and 164.1 > 146.1 for NAC and 167.1 > 123.0 and 167.1 > 149.0 for d3-NAC. Plasma malondialdehyde was determined after derivatization with thiobarbituric acid following separation by RP-HPLC followed and subsequent fluorescence detection as described by [
22
] with modifications [
23
]. The analyses of protein carbonyls and 3-nitrotyrosine in plasma by two in-house ELISA methods have been described elsewhere [
23
,
24
]. Protein concentration was measured by the Bradford method prior to the respective ELISAs.
Histomorphometrical analysis of mouse placenta
Placentas of one male and one female for each dam were fixed in paraformaldehyde solution 4% in PBS, stored in 80% ethyl alcohol, sliced transversally through their center with a scalpel, embedded in paraffin by tissue processor (Shandon Excelsior ES, Thermo Scientific), cut into 5 µm sections using the Microm HM 325 (Thermo Scientific) and stained with hematoxylin-eosin. Image analysis system (Nis-Elements Br) applied to the optical microscope (Nikon Microphot FX) was used for quantitative histomorphometrical analyses. Thickness of layers (i.e., decidua basalis, junctional zone and labyrinth) was measured using three serial sections/sample [
25
].
Proteomics, lipidomics and metabolomics profiles of placental samples
Placentas from one male and one female from each pregnant dam were selected, for a total of 3 males and 3 females per experimental group. Samples were lyophilized, homogenized and subjected to methyl-tert-butyl ether/methanol extraction of lipids, metabolites and proteins [
26
]. Protein pellets were enzymatically digested and run in triplicate in data-independent mode (DIA) using an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Raw files were run on FragPipe 21.0 [
27
]. Further details on protein extraction and proteomic analysis are reported in
Supplementary Material
; mass spectrometry raw files, database, libraries, fragpipe-workflow, experiment annotation file and DIA-NN output folder are available at:
ftp://massive.ucsd.edu/v06/MSV000092388
. Metabolites and lipids extracted from the same samples were analyzed by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy analysis, see
Supplementary Material
for further details.
Bioinformatic analysis of proteomics data
DIA-NN output was pre-processed with DEP v1.12.0 [
28
] in R 4.0.4 as previously described [
29
], except for missing value imputation which was performed by the quantile regression-based left-censored function (“QRILC”). Correction of the batch effect was performed with RUVSeq v1.24.0 setting k = 7 in R [
30
]. Differential expression analysis was performed with edgeR v3.32.1 [
31
] comparing each condition versus their basal control (CTR/CD) for each sex, and controlling for the False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 5%. A complete list of differential expressed protein (DEPs) is reported in
Supplementary Material
; overlapping of DEPs across conditions was visualized using ggVenn v0.1.10 and UpSetR v1.4.0. KEGG enrichment analysis was performed by querying DEPs in ClueGO v.2.5.10 within Cytoscape 3.10.1 [
32
,
33
], considering significant pathways with
p
< 0.05 following Benjamini-Hotchberg correction. To investigate associations with selected classes of diseases, mouse gene identifiers, encoding for DEPs, were transformed into human orthologues by the g:Orth tool within g:Profiler (
https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost
) [
34
] and used in the DisGeNet app v.7.3.0 [
35
] in Cytoscape setting score ≥ 0.3, evidence index ≥ 0.5, and “Biomarker” as association type. Nutritional and Metabolic Diseases, as well as Nervous System Diseases, Behaviour and Behaviour Mechanism and Mental Disorders were inspected, merging the results of these last three into a single network. Only diseases associated to at least five genes were kept. ggplot2 v3.5.1 [
36
] was used to visualize results from KEGGs and DisGeNet.
Gene expression on fetal brains and amniotic fluid
The genetic sex of pups was determined by Sly/Xlr PCR [
37
]. Fetal brains of one male and one female from each pregnant dam were selected, for a total of 6 males and 6 females per experimental group. Total RNAs from fetal brains and amniotic fluids were isolated as described in
Supplementary Material
. cDNA was reverse transcribed from 1 µg of RNA using the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit and the Gene Amp PCR System 9700 (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Real-time PCR was performed using the AB 7500 Real-Time PCR System, with TaqMan master mix and TaqMan™Gene Expression Assays (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Table
S1
). All samples were run in duplicate. The relative expression level of each mRNA (normalized to Hprt used as the housekeeping gene, and relative to the appropriate male mice vehicle group) was calculated using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.4.1 (GraphPad Software, USA) or JMP 10 (SAS Institute Inc., USA). The sample size was calculated through the G*Power 3.1 software (
www.gpower.hhu.de
). Bartlett’s and Shapiro-Wilk tests were used to test homogeneity of variances among groups and normal distribution of data, respectively. Maternal parameters were analyzed using a two-way ANOVA with stressful condition (PNS/CTRL or HFD/CD) and treatment (NAC/Vehicle) as between-subject factors and repeated measure (i.e., body weight) as within-subject factors, followed by post-hoc Šídák’s multiple comparisons test, except in the case of repeated measures where Tukey’s test was used as it provides more statistical power. Placental morphological data and gene expression data were analyzed through a three-way ANOVA with prenatal condition (PNS/CTRL or HFD/CD), treatment (NAC/Vehicle) and sex (F/M) as between-subject factors, followed by post-hoc Šídák’s multiple comparisons test. Lipidomics and metabolomics data were analyzed by performing Generalized Linear Models considering prenatal condition (PNS/CTRL or HFD/CD), treatment (NAC/Vehicle) and sex (F/M) as interaction factors. Data were graphically presented as mean ± SEM. Grubb’s test, using 5% significance level critical values, was used to detect outliers [
38
]. A level of probability set a
p
< 0.05 was used as statistically significant.

Introduction
Both maternal obesity and maternal psychological stress hold similar risks for neurodevelopment in the progeny, leading to increased susceptibility to mental disorders [
1
–
4
]. Several clinical studies have reported that mothers experiencing psychological or metabolic stress during pregnancy are characterized by chronic low-grade systemic inflammation and increased oxidative stress, leading to an overall suboptimal intrauterine environment with overlapping long-term outcomes [
5
–
7
]. We have recently described overlapping sex-dependent negative outcomes in adolescent mouse offspring either exposed to prenatal stress (PNS) or maternal high-fat diet (mHFD), unraveling a greater inflammatory and oxidative burden in the hippocampus of female subjects [
8
]. Given this evidence, in the present study, we aimed to assess whether changes in oxidative stress and inflammation represent early manifestations of prenatal adversities and whether antioxidants may be used as an innovative mechanism-based early therapeutic strategy [
9
,
10
]. Among the many antioxidants, N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), which is a thiol-containing compound deriving from the amino acid cysteine, acts as a scavenger of free radicals and holds the potential to modulate inflammation and brain neurotransmission [
11
].
In this study we focused on the short-term effects of either PNS or mHFD specifically on placenta and fetal brain evaluating whether maternal administration of NAC might act as a preventive strategy. Since the placenta may ultimately convey “toxic stress” signals deriving from distinct adverse prenatal conditions to the fetal brain through the placenta-brain axis [
12
–
14
], we thoroughly investigated its role by performing untargeted proteomic, lipidomic and metabolomic, in combination with histomorphological analysis. Moreover, in a translational approach, we also tested the effects of NAC on the inflammatory/redox unbalance in amniotic fluid and maternal plasma. In fetal brains, we assessed oxidative stress as well as inflammatory and macrophage/microglia-related markers. Worth mentioning, during fetal development, placental macrophages, the precursors of many tissue-resident macrophages including microglial cells, migrate from the yolk sac to the fetal brain [
15
]. In maternal obesity, these cells are exposed to the same pro-inflammatory/pro-oxidant maternal signals that may induce microglia aberrant activation. Since microglia are involved in synaptic pruning, an increased activation during sensitive developmental stages may affect synapse maturation leading to synaptic loss. Interestingly, patients diagnosed with schizophrenia or depression show a reduction in grey matter volume, compatible with excessive synaptic elimination [
9
,
16
], supporting the hypothesis that early aberrant activation of microglia may contribute to set the stage for increased vulnerability to neuropsychiatric disorders later in life.

To get further insights on the possible impact of PNS and mHFD as risk factors for disease pathogenesis, we investigated gene-disease associations using the DisGeNet database, for each DEP list concerning Metabolic/Nutritional Diseases and Neurological/Behavioral Diseases.
With regard to metabolic/nutritional diseases, we found that obesity was associated with many genes encoding DEPs across all conditions, except for HFD-Veh and HFD-NAC female placentas for which we found no associations with any disease. A high number of associations was found with neurological/behavioral disorders. Metabolomic and lipidomic analysis
Due to the limited number of samples per group and the between-subjects variability, no metabolite was significantly different in a specific condition compared to the corresponding control, for each sex. However, we found that the PNS had a higher impact on levels of aqueous metabolites. In particular, a main effect of treatment (Veh/NAC) was found for amino acids such as phenylalanine, tyrosine, aspartate, glutamate valine, leucine, isoleucine, histidine, phospholipid metabolites (myo-inositol, choline), pyruvate and TCA cycle metabolism (succinate, acetate, lactate) and metabolites linked to redox balance (glutathione) (Table
S3
for statistical details), all displaying lower levels in NAC-treated mice than in Veh. This was especially evident in males, since a significant sex x treatment interaction was obtained for most of these metabolites except for aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine). In addition, also the lipid PC yielded the same sex x treatment significant interaction, but with males having higher values in NAC-treated subjects than in Veh. Furthermore, a significant stress x sex interaction was found for most of the metabolites belonging to the pathways analyzed (glucose metabolism, pyruvate and TCA cycle, phospholipid and redox balance), with opposite effects of PNS in males and females. A significant diet x sex interaction was observed in the mHFD group, only for aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine and tyrosine) levels. In addition, a significant effect of the diet was observed for PC and linoleic acid, with higher values in the mHFD group.

Discussion
In this study we tested the hypothesis that different prenatal stressors could act through evolutionarily conserved mechanisms, such as oxidative stress and inflammation, to affect brain and behavioral development in the offspring. Starting from this hypothesis, we investigated the protective effects of the antioxidant NAC in two animal models of PNS and mHFD, using a multi-disciplinary approach. In particular, we combined proteomic, metabolomic, lipidomic and histological analysis to characterize the structural and functional changes at the levels of the placenta, while targeted gene expression analysis was carried out in the brains of male and female fetuses.
Oxidative stress emerged as a common mechanism affecting the maternal environment, as we found circulating 3-Nitrotyrosine levels, a marker of nitro-oxidation, to be increased by both PNS and mHFD, with NAC administration preventing such alteration. NAC also prevented body weight gain during pregnancy, possibly through a reduction of reactive oxygen species, which are essential during adipocyte differentiation [
39
,
40
] (see Fig.
6
for a graphical summary of the main results).
Fig. 6
Main sex-dependent effects following PNS or mHFD.
Both stressors increased systemic oxidative stress markers in the pregnant mother, an effect moderated by NAC. During prenatal life, greater sex-dependent effects characterised placental physiology in males and brain gene expression in females. Arrows pointing up indicate increasing - while arrows pointing down decreasing - effects on the outcomes. Rescuing effects of the prenatal administration of NAC are marked by a blue tick.
Oxidative stress signals may reach the growing fetus through the placenta, thwarting developmental trajectories. We have previously shown that both PNS and mHFD negatively affect placental physiology [
41
,
42
]. In this study, we assessed the effects of these stressors on placental structure. One fundamental compartment of the placenta is the junctional zone [
43
]. Previous data suggest a specific role for this layer as an early sensor of nutritional status, with male fetuses being more vulnerable to metabolic challenges compared to females [
44
]. In agreement with these data, we show that mHFD increased the thickness of the junctional zone, in males only, an effect that was prevented by prenatal NAC. In clinical practice, a thickened placenta is associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes and neonatal morbidity related to a variety of maternal conditions, including obesity and diabetes [
45
]. Moreover, independently from sex, PNS significantly reduced the thickness of the labyrinth, another zone playing a key role in nutrient exchange: such layer represents a target of placental stressors, leading to impaired materno-fetal transfer across the placental barrier [
46
].
Placental transfer of nutrients and metabolites relies upon endocytosis through, among others, clathrin-mediated mechanisms [
47
]. Our proteomic analysis interestingly showed the induction of clathrin light chain proteins and dynamins within the
Endocytosis
pathway specifically in the PNS group, suggesting a compensatory mechanism due to the reduced size of the labyrinth layer. Overall our proteomic data are in agreement with recent reports on the human placental transcriptome and proteome induced by maternal stressors, where
Endocytosis
, together with
Thermogenesis
, have been found as highly enriched pathways affecting basic signaling cascades involved in fetal development [
48
,
49
]. For both pathways, a main role of mTOR (a crucial nutrient sensor highly expressed in the placenta) has been described [
50
,
51
]. These data indicate that both stressors disrupt nutrient transfer mechanisms, thwarting fetal developmental trajectories.
Converging sex-specific effects were found following PNS and mHFD in male placental proteome, where the same pathways (e.g.:
Huntington’s Disease, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
) showed downregulation in those DEPs involved in oxidative phosphorylation, including NADH dehydrogenases, in line with previous evidence showing redox imbalance and disrupted mitochondrial respiration in male fetuses from obese women [
52
]. This downregulation was prevented by NAC. Furthermore, male placentas also showed converging effects of PNS and mHFD when an association analysis with Neurological/Behavioral Disorders was performed. We found specific modulation of proteins associated with Schizophrenia, Intellectual disability, Bipolar disorder and Mood disorders. Among these, we identified ANK3 extending our previous results showing a role for this gene in embedding early stressful events in brain function [
53
]. We also identified SIRT1 which is involved in the inflammatory/redox signaling cascades [
54
]. In this regard, recent evidence suggests that the downregulation of SIRT1 by mHFD might hold a risk factor for later-life cardio-metabolic disorders, specifically in males [
55
,
56
].
Overall, both stressors were found to affect the structure of the placenta, although acting on different layers. The analysis of placental proteome indicated that PNS showed stronger effects. When a convergence between mHFD and PNS was found, this was mediated by the male sex and was related to oxidative stress pathways and reverted by NAC. A convergence between these two stressors was also found in the association analysis with Neurological/Behavioral Disorders where proteins involved in early embedding of adverse events were captured by the analysis.
Similarly to proteomics, metabolomics showed a greater impact of PNS in males, having higher levels of most of the metabolites compared to females. In HFD mice, only minor changes were observed. Importantly, NAC prevented more effectively the effects of PNS, decreasing the levels of several metabolites.
An increased pro-oxidant maternal environment may also have direct consequences on fetal brain development. We have previously shown a sex-dependent increase of inflammation and oxidative stress in the brain of adolescent offspring following mHFD and PNS, with stronger effects in females. Here, we sought to investigate whether such derangements are already present during fetal life.
To this regard, we performed a targeted gene expression analysis of the fetal brain which revealed greater effects in females, especially following mHFD. We found increased levels of
Il-1β
both upon PNS and mHFD and increased
Il-6
as a result of PNS, mirroring the effects - previously shown - of maternal immune activation [
57
,
58
]. Elevated
Il-6
levels in the fetal brain have been associated with increased glutamatergic synapse density and disruption of hippocampal connectivity in adult mice [
59
], in addition to an increased risk for neuropsychiatric diseases in humans, supporting a main role for this cytokine in shaping brain development [
60
]. Interestingly, when evaluating markers related to microglial homeostasis and redox balance, we observed more pervasive effects resulting from mHFD exposure rather than PNS. In particular, mHFD upregulated gene expression of growth factors (i.e.,
Tgf-β
and
Igf-1
) and markers relevant for microglia activation (i.e.:,
Cd 68
and
Tmem 119
), specifically in female fetal brains, possibly contributing to later alterations in neuronal pruning and function. These data confirm and expand previous findings observed in mHFD models [
61
,
62
]. Moreover, mHFD drove the fetal brain towards a pro-oxidant profile by decreasing
Ucp-2
and increasing the
iNOS/Arg-1
ratio. To this regard, it is important to mention that iNOS and Arg-1 are mainly produced by microglia/macrophages in the brain and changes in their expression have been associated with derangements in brain development [
63
]. These data confirm that sex-dependent changes previously observed in adolescent females, as a result of mHFD, are already present in fetal brain and are potentially linked to changes in microglia development. We cannot exclude that other mechanisms could also be at play, including changes in maternal microbiota, which is affected by maternal diet, as previously described [
64
].
Overall, both PNS and mHFD impinged upon shared inflammatory/redox-related pathways. The ability of NAC to prevent the increase in
Il-6
and
iNOS/Arg-1
supports the main role played by inflammation and oxidative stress in mediating the effects of prenatal adversities on neurodevelopment and supports preventive strategies based on buffering oxidative stress. Of note, we observed in the amniotic fluid an immune-inflammatory state similar to that observed in fetal brains, with NAC administration being able to protect the homeostasis of the intrauterine milieu.
In conclusion, our study provides further support to the “funnel effect” model whereby different prenatal adverse conditions converge on evolutionarily conserved pathways, increasing vulnerability for adult diseases [
10
]. Overall, data gathered so far indicate that prenatal adversities may enhance the physiological sex differences in neurodevelopmental trajectories underlying unique sex-specific responses to the same exposures. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is that male development requires that less energy is allocated to placental reserves, in favor of rapid body growth. This causes male fetuses to “live dangerously in the womb” when facing early challenges [
65
,
66
], making this sex more vulnerable to diseases with a metabolic component. These data are also consistent with previous findings showing greater vulnerability of male’ placentas in a mouse model of maternal immune activation [
67
]. In contrast, despite the placentls apparent preserved functionality, females experience their own unique developmental response, with increased brain inflammation and oxidative stress, similar to what we have observed during adolescence [
8
]. Given the interconnection between inflammation and oxidative stress, therapeutic strategies that can modulate both processes are highly desirable. To this regard, notwithstanding the sex differences induced by the different prenatal stressors, NAC was able to restore some of these effects, acting on shared mechanisms underlying multiple environmental challenges, a notion that, if translated to the clinic, could improve the health of pregnant women at risk [
5
].
The sex-dependent patterns described are consistent with the sex-specific disease trajectories showing increased cardio-metabolic risk in males and greater susceptibility to mood disorders in females and support a prenatal origin of differential embedding of adverse experiences in different fetal organs.
